displayQuote: We can only be said to be alive in the moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure

meta.title: Who really said "We can only be said to be alive in the moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wilder wrote it — in The Woman of Andros (1930). The printed line reads “those moments,” and it does not stop there.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We can only be said to be alive in the moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Wilder, lightly edited. Chrysis says it in The Woman of Andros (1930) — “those moments,” singular “treasure.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Wilder wrote it, in The Woman of Andros (1930) — but it is one word off, and the sentence does not end where the internet ends it. Chrysis says it while telling her dinner guests about a dead hero allowed to relive a single ordinary day. The printed text reads “in those moments,” and runs straight on: “for our hearts are not strong enough to love every moment.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: February 1930 · Albert & Charles Boni, New York
inside the story Chrysis tells her guests on the island of Brynos
Chrysis — of a hero given one day of his life back

source.excerpt: “My friends,” continued Chrysis, turning her eyes slowly from face to face, “as he awoke in his boyhood’s room, pain filled his heart — not only because it had started beating again, but because he saw the walls of his home and knew that in a moment he would see his parents who lay long since in the earth of that country. … Suddenly the hero saw that the living too are dead and that we can only be said to be alive in those moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure; for our hearts are not strong enough to love every moment.”
trail: February 1930 — the novel appears from Albert & Charles Boni. The first-edition scan at the Internet Archive ↗ carries the notice “COPYRIGHT, 1930, BY ALBERT & CHARLES BONI, INC.” and prints the passage as quoted above.

23 February 2026 — with the book out of US copyright, Project Gutenberg publishes a proofread transcription ↗, credited to the Online Distributed Proofreading Team working from Internet Archive images. It reads “in those moments … conscious of our treasure” — a second set of eyes on the same words.
Wikiquote lists the line under The Woman of Andros (1930) ↗ and gets the work right, but prints “our treasures.” Both texts above read the singular.
source.excerptNote: The semicolon is doing the work. Wilder is not recommending that we stay conscious of our treasure — the clause after it says we cannot, and the hero in the story lasts under an hour before begging to be let out of the day he asked for.

author.name: Thornton Wilder
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1897–1975 · American novelist & playwright · three Pulitzer Prizes
author.bio: Thornton Wilder was born in Madison, Wisconsin, in 1897 and won three Pulitzer Prizes — for The Bridge of San Luis Rey in 1928, then for the plays Our Town (1938) and The Skin of Our Teeth (1943). The Woman of Andros, his third novel, moved him back into the ancient world at the moment his American readers most wanted him in theirs, and it is where his run of uncritical acclaim ended.

copyAttribution: “We can only be said to be alive in those moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure; for our hearts are not strong enough to love every moment.” — Thornton Wilder, The Woman of Andros (New York: Albert & Charles Boni, 1930), spoken by Chrysis. The circulating version reads “in the moments” and stops at “treasure”.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in the quoting
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this sentence — it is Wilder’s, and the work it comes from is correctly named almost everywhere. What travels is a lightly edited version of it, cut loose from the clause that explains it.

items.why: Both the 1930 first edition ↗ and the Gutenberg transcription ↗ read “in those moments” — pointing back at the moments the story has just described, rather than stating a general rule.
The plural is what Wikiquote ↗ prints, and it has been copied widely from there. Both the first edition and the proofread transcription have the singular, “our treasure.”

items.who: Wilder stating a maxim in his own voice
items.why: It is Chrysis — a character, at a dinner party, inside a story she is telling — describing what a dead man understood when he was given one day back. And the sentence carries on past the full stop the quotation invents: “for our hearts are not strong enough to love every moment.”

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence as printed: “Suddenly the hero saw that the living too are dead and that we can only be said to be alive in those moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure; for our hearts are not strong enough to love every moment.” — The Woman of Andros ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Chrysis keeps a house on the invented Greek island of Brynos and feeds young men dinner, and this is one of the stories she tells them. A hero begs Zeus for a single day of his life back. He is granted the least eventful day he ever lived — on the condition that he live it as two people at once, the boy doing it and the man who already knows how it all ends. He sees his mother at the loom, his father crossing the courtyard, and inside the hour he is asking the gods to release him.

That is the setting for the sentence people now print on its own. It is not advice to notice your treasure more; it is the reason the hero could not stand to. The novel was the third-best-selling book in the United States in 1930, and also the first of Wilder’s to be seriously attacked — Wikipedia’s article on the novel ↗ records that Mike Gold’s review in The New Republic faulted him for not addressing modern social issues.
detailsBody: Wilder took his starting point from Roman comedy. The novel’s own copyright page states that “the first part of this novel is based upon the Andria, a comedy of Terence who in turn based his work upon two Greek plays, now lost to us, by Menander.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Project Gutenberg ebook #78024 (“The woman of Andros”, Thornton Wilder) states “Original publication: New York: Albert & Charles Boni, 1930” and “Release date: February 23, 2026”, and its text reads “we can only be said to be alive in those moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasure; for our hearts are not strong enough to love every moment.”

The scanned 1930 first edition carries “COPYRIGHT, 1930, BY ALBERT & CHARLES BONI, INC.” and the same sentence, in the same wording — “those moments”, singular “treasure” — inside the story Chrysis tells.
Wikiquote lists the line under The Woman of Andros (1930), based on Terence's Andria, but prints “our treasures” (plural).

Wikipedia gives the publisher as Albert & Charles Boni, release date February 1930, records it as the third-best selling book in the United States in 1930, and states that Mike Gold's review in The New Republic faulted Wilder for not addressing modern social issues, the first significant negative critical response to his work.

Wikipedia states: “All works (excepting sound recordings) first published or released in the United States before January 1, 1931, have lost their copyright protection 95 years later, effective January 1, 2026.”
Wikipedia gives Thornton Wilder's dates as born April 17, 1897 and died December 7, 1975, with Pulitzer Prizes for the Novel (1928) and for Drama (1938, 1943).
